[[File:Fossombroni - Saggio di ricerche sull'intensità del lume, 1781 - 1523971.jpg|thumb|''Saggio'', 1781]]
'''Vittorio Fossombroni''' (15 September 1754{{snd}}13 April 1844) was an Italian [[politician|statesman]], [[mathematician]], [[economist]] and a distinguished drainage [[engineer]].<ref name="auto">{{cite book |last= Beales |first= Derek |author-link= |date= 6 Jun 2014|title= The Risorgimento and the Unification of Italy | url= https://books.google.com/books?id=CswFBAAAQBAJ |access-date=13 February 2022|location= Oxon| publisher= Routledge| page= 35| isbn= 978-1-317-87857-5}}</ref>

==Biography==
Fossombroni was born at [[Arezzo]].<ref name="auto1">{{cite book |last= Capecchi |first= Danilo |author-link= |date= 11 May 2012|title= History of Virtual Work Laws: A History of Mechanics Prospective | url= https://books.google.com/books?id=8qUXV6lo8-wC|access-date=13 February 2022|location= Berlin| publisher= Springer Science & Business Media | page= 300| isbn= 978-88-470-2056-6}}</ref> He was educated at the [[University of Pisa]], where he devoted himself particularly to [[mathematics]] and [[hydraulics]]. He obtained an official appointment in [[Tuscany]] in 1782, and twelve years later was entrusted by the [[grand duke]] with the direction of the works for the drainage of the marshy [[Valdichiana]], one of the four valleys around [[Arezzo]], on which subject he had published a treatise in 1789.<ref name="EB1911">{{EB1911|inline=y|wstitle=Fossombroni, Vittorio, Count|volume=10|page=732|first=Luigi|last=Villari|author-link=Luigi Villari}}</ref>

In 1796 he was made minister for foreign affairs, but on the [[France|French]] occupation of Tuscany in 1799 he fled to [[Sicily]]. On the erection of the grand duchy into the ephemeral [[Kingdom of Etruria]], under the queen-regent [[Marie Louise, Duchess of Parma|Maria Louise]], he was, appointed president of the commission of finance. In 1809 he went to [[Paris]] as one of the [[senator]]s for Tuscany to pay homage to [[Napoleon I of France|Napoleon]].<ref name="EB1911"/>

On the restoration of the [[Ferdinand III, Grand Duke of Tuscany|Grand Duke Ferdinand III]] in 1814, he was made president of the legislative commission and was appointed prime minister, a position he retained under the [[Leopold II, Grand Duke of Tuscany|Grand Duke Leopold II]].<ref>{{cite book |last= Graça |first= J. Da |author-link= |date= 13 Feb 2017|title= Heads of State and Government | url= https://books.google.com/books?id=M0YfDgAAQBAJ|access-date=13 February 2022|location= New York City| publisher= Springer | page= 497| isbn= 978-1-349-65771-1}}</ref> He was an important representative of the Italian School of virtual work laws.<ref name="auto1"/> When he was prime minister, he pursued a policy of laissez-faire and international free trade.<ref name="auto"/>

According to Luigi Villaris, writing in the [[Encyclopædia Britannica Eleventh Edition|''Encyclopædia Britannica'' Eleventh Edition]]: "His administration, which was only terminated by his death, greatly contributed to promote the well-being of the country. He was the real master of Tuscany, and the bases of his rule were equality of all subjects before the law, honesty in the administration of justice and toleration of opinion, but he totally neglected the moral improvement of the people."<ref name="EB1911"/>

Fossombroni married at the age of seventy-eight.<ref name="EB1911"/> His son [[Enrico Vittorio Fossombroni]] was a Senator in the [[unification of Italy|Kingdom of Italy]].{{Citation needed|date=September 2018}}

Vittorio Fossombroni died at [[Florence]] in 1844.
